records.title: Parallelizing Instruction Scheduling for the GPU on the GPU
records.summary: In this article, we describe how to use the GPU to parallelize a precise search-based algorithm for solving the instruction scheduling problem for a GPU target. Instruction scheduling for the GPU is a multi-objective optimization problem in which the challenge lies in balancing the conflicting objectives of minimizing register pressure (RP) and maximizing instruction-level parallelism (ILP). We solve this problem using a precise algorithm that is based on Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), which is a nature-inspired intelligent-search technique that has been used to compute precise solutions to NP-hard problems in operations research (OR). Such intelligent-search techniques were not used in the past to solve NP-hard compiler optimization problems, because they require substantially more computation than the heuristic techniques used in production compilers. In this article, we show that parallelizing such a technique on the GPU does not only make it reasonably practical for compilation, but it also makes it possible to simultaneously explore different ways of balancing RP and ILP. Different groups of GPU threads search for solutions that balance RP and ILP differently, and then the most balanced solution is selected based on a certain cost function. We also describe a number of techniques that we developed to efficiently parallelize an ACO algorithm for solving this multi-objective optimization problem on the GPU. The experimental evaluation shows that parallel ACO-based scheduling on the GPU runs up to 21 times faster than sequential ACO-based scheduling on the CPU, and this leads to reducing the total compile time of the rocPRIM benchmarks by 42%. ACO-based scheduling improves the execution speed of the compiled benchmarks by up to 72% relative to AMD’s production scheduler. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first successful attempt to parallelize a compiler optimization algorithm on the GPU.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Optimizing Deep Neural Network Sparse Kernels on Multi-core CPUs
records.summary: Vector-wise pruning is widely used to reduce the inference cost of deep neural networks (DNNs), but it turns key operators into sparse convolution (SpConv) and sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM) kernels that are difficult to optimize on multi-core CPUs. Although prior sparse-kernel acceleration has largely centered on GPUs, CPUs remain a first-order inference platform in CPU-only deployments and in heterogeneous serving when GPUs are scarce or memory-constrained. We present TurboSparse, an approach for accelerating vector-wise sparse DNN kernels on modern multi-core CPUs. TurboSparse (1) eliminates im2col by executing SpConv directly over a DNN-oriented sparse format to reduce data movement and improve reuse, (2) introduces row-merging micro-kernels guided by an analytical SIMD-utilization model to increase vector-lane occupancy, and (3) fuses consecutive sparse kernels when their combined working set fits in private caches to reuse intermediates and cut memory traffic. Across four CPUs (x86 and ARM) and representative pruned DNN workloads, TurboSparse outperforms five expert-tuned CPU libraries, achieving up to 4.05 × speedup for consecutive SpConvs and sustaining 15–80% of each processor’s theoretical peak throughput.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: A Fairness-Aware Management for Multi-Tier Storage Systems
records.summary: Modern cloud storage systems serve multiple tenants with diverse I/O behaviors and make fairness under shared resource contention a critical requirement. To mitigate the random-write limitations of high-capacity Shingled-Magnetic-Recording (SMR) disks, hybrid multi-tier architectures are widely adopted. However, ensuring fairness in such systems remains challenging because cache optimization and SMR cleaning mitigation constitute fundamentally different bottlenecks that evolve over distinct time scales. This paper presents a fairness-aware management for multi-tier storage systems by integrating a DRAM cache, a flash-based persistent cache, and an SMR backend. By explicitly decoupling short-term cache contention from long-term cleaning interference, the proposed method applies tier-specific priority management to regulate hit rate degradation and cleaning slowdown in a coordinated manner across the storage hierarchy. Experimental results on ten mixed workloads show that the proposed method improves integrated fairness by up to 4.59 × while reducing average response time and P99.9 long-tail latency by up to 11.4% and 15.2%, respectively.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: vMiG: A Fast and NUMA-Aware Virtualized GPU Migration System via Pipelined Zero-Copy Data Paths
records.summary: GPUs have become indispensable infrastructure for cloud platforms, powering workloads from large-model inference to real-time rendering, and the transition to cloud-native GPU computing is accelerating. One of the key challenges in this transition is live migration, which is essential for enabling transparent workload relocation for load balancing, fault tolerance, and resource consolidation. However, GPU virtualization introduces a critical migration bottleneck rooted in the mediated pass-through (MPT) migration stack: massive device state, particularly VRAM footprints scaling into tens of gigabytes, must be exported through vendor-controlled interfaces whose buffering, copying, and placement behavior limits high-throughput VRAM streaming in practice. To address this challenge, we propose vMiG , a framework that first characterizes why the MPT migration data path is poorly matched to high-throughput VRAM streaming. vMiG then uses this analysis to restructure the migration pipeline for higher VRAM transfer throughput and shorter blackout time, through zero-copy data movement, end-to-end pipelining, and non-uniform memory access (NUMA)-aware control path placement. Evaluations show that NUMA-aware controller placement improves VRAM migration throughput by 58.8%, while copy-path optimizations reduce memory copies from seven to near the theoretical minimum of four. Together, these optimizations achieve VRAM migration throughput up to 5.19 × the baseline rate and reduce end-to-end migration time by up to 58% for VRAM-intensive AI workloads.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: PPT-GPU 2.0: A Validated, Accurate, and Scalable Modeling of NVIDIA GPUs
records.summary: Performance modeling and simulation tools (ModSim) for GPUs continue to be indispensable for performance optimization and a deeper understanding of their complex behaviors and architectures. We detail PPT-GPU 2.0, highlighting significant updates and improvements to PPT-GPU. These include a detailed modeling of the Ampere architecture, including shared memory and tensor cores, while extending coverage across Volta, Turing, and Ampere. Furthermore, we introduce a new GPU occupancy model, “Balance Model”. New performance metrics are also incorporated, including the maximum/minimum number of blocks executed concurrently per streaming Multiprocessor, and the active cycles for each execution pipeline. We evaluate PPT-GPU 2.0 on A100 GPUs, an Ampere architecture. We validate the results using a diverse set of benchmarks compared against real hardware, utilizing NVIDIA Nsight Compute, Accel-Sim (a cycle-accurate simulator), and HyFiSS. PPT-GPU 2.0 demonstrates notable accuracy improvements. For instance, it achieves an average error of 16.4% for active cycles, 9.3% for standard execution pipelines and 5.7% for tensor cores, while maintaining high accuracy for memory hierarchy (8% L1, 21.4% L2 hit rates, and 16.4% for IPC) and execution pipeline modeling. It achieves a 33.51x speedup in simulation time compared with Accel-Sim.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Dynamic-size Superblock Management based on Buddy System for Modern SSDs
records.summary: Superblocks are widely used in SSDs to exploit internal parallelism thus improving I/O throughput. Although dynamic-size superblock schemes enhance space utilization for varied workloads, they introduce internal fragmentation and impact overall performance. To address this issue, we propose Buddy , a novel dynamic-size superblock management scheme based on the buddy system, which adapts to I/O patterns by dynamically splitting and merging superblocks. This approach maintains large blocks to preserve parallelism for sequential writes and generates smaller blocks on demand to handle random writes effectively. We further introduce the expansion GC mechanism to adaptively adjust GC unit size based on I/O intensity and GC efficiency for alleviating fragmentation and preserving SSD parallelism. Trace-driven evaluations with real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our approach can reduce average I/O latency and GC-induced data migration by 47.0 % and 24.5 %, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art superblock management techniques.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
records.summary: Machine learning models excel across applications like medical diagnostics, weather forecasting, natural language processing and autonomous driving, yet their inadequate handling of uncertainty remains crucial for safety-critical applications. Traditional neural networks fail to recognize out-of-domain (OOD) data, often producing incorrect predictions without indicating uncertainty. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for uncertainty estimation by providing statistically grounded probabilities alongside predictions. Despite these advantages, BNNs suffer from high computational costs in both training and prediction. Predictions require sampling over weight distributions and multiple forward passes. To address this challenge, the Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) serves as an extreme approximation of Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI). While SVI assumes Gaussian-distributed weights without restrictions on activations, PFP extends this assumption to activations. This enables a fully analytical uncertainty propagation, replacing multiple forward passes with a single, more complex forward pass operating on probability distributions. Thus, PFP requires specialized Gaussian-propagating operators absent from standard deep learning libraries. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compilation, optimization, and deployment of PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. By implementing custom operators in the deep learning compiler TVM, we develop a dedicated operator library for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Multiple operator implementations, along with manual and automatic tuning techniques, are applied to maximize efficiency. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency. For small mini-batch sizes, critical for low-latency applications, our approach achieves speedups of up to 3900 ×. Our results show that PFP-based BNNs achieve performance comparable to SVI-BNNs for uncertainty disentanglement on the Dirty-MNIST dataset and for complex OOD detection on CIFAR-10 against SVHN, all while significantly reducing computational overhead. These findings underscore the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation and operator tuning to accelerate BNN predictions and enable their efficient deployment on resource-constrained embedded systems.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: A Host-CSD Collaborative Framework for High-Performance LSM-Based KV Stores
records.summary: LSM-based key-value stores are widely used due to their write efficiency and scalability. However, their background compaction process requires substantial data movement between the host and storage devices, resulting in inefficient resource usage, frequent write stalls, and degraded overall throughput. Existing optimizations fail to address the performance bottlenecks caused by excessive system interconnect traffic. Although in-storage computing offers a promising way to mitigate data transfer overhead, prior works typically offload all compaction tasks blindly to computational storage devices. Our preliminary experiments show that such naive offloading leads to performance inefficiency due to CSD resource constraints. In this work, we propose CSD-CoKV + , a host-CSD collaborative framework that enables efficient compaction acceleration for LSM-based KV stores. Specifically, we design a semantic-aware offloader to selectively dispatch suitable compaction jobs to CSDs, together with a lightweight FPGA-based compaction kernel for efficient in-storage execution under constrained device resources. In addition, we develop a range-partitioned data organization with two-level load balancing to preserve locality and improve scalability across CSD arrays, and further introduce a host-device hierarchical cache to better exploit device-level locality in the read path. Evaluations on a real SmartSSD-based prototype show that, with the default host-only baseline, CSD-CoKV + improves write throughput by up to 2.26 × and boosts compaction throughput by up to 3.42 ×, while improving read throughput by up to 28.5%.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Exposing Embedded Matrix Multiplication with polyhedral transformations for CGRA compilation
records.summary: Matrix-matrix multiplication ( mmul ) is a dominant computing pattern in edge workloads, but in real applications it is often embedded within larger affine programs and intertwined with other operations. Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Arrays (CGRAs) can flexibly and efficiently support it, since they combine operation-level reconfigurability and high energy efficiency. However, mapping computational kernels that include mmul with state-of-the-art compilation strategies often leads to suboptimal results, since its multi-dimensional structure hampers the uncovering of its inherent parallelism and, ultimately, runtime performance. This paper presents Kernel-CGRA, a compiler flow that uses polyhedral transformations to expose legal affine mmul subspaces, lower each accepted region to a back-end-independent operation, and preserve the surrounding computation in the generic CDFG path. For CGRA execution, the operation is instantiated as a parametric output-stationary kernel, while residual regions are reconnected through context generation and live-value preservation. The matcher is intentionally strict: only regions proven to match the supported affine mmul form are rewritten. Across canonical, fused, and application-level benchmarks, Kernel-CGRA achieves runtime speedups of up to 10.2 × over state-of-the-art CGRA CDFG compilation with modulo scheduling and loop unrolling.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Denoising Application Performance Models with Noise-Resilient Priors
records.summary: As parallel codes are scaled to larger computing systems, performance models play a crucial role in identifying potential bottlenecks. However, constructing these models analytically is often challenging. Empirical models based on performance measurements provide a practical alternative, but measurements on high-performance computing (HPC) systems are frequently affected by noise, which can lead to misleading predictions. To mitigate the impact of noise, we introduce application-specific effort-based priors into the modeling process. These priors are derived from noise-resilient measurements of computational effort, combined with domain knowledge about common algorithms used in communication routines. By incorporating these priors, we effectively constrain the model’s search space, eliminating complexity classes that capture noise rather than true performance characteristics. This approach keeps the models closely aligned with theoretical expectations and substantially enhances their predictive accuracy. Moreover, it reduces experimental overhead by cutting the number of repeated measurements by half.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: UnifaSVD: A Unified and Fast Framework of Singular Value Decomposition on GPU Architectures
records.summary: Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a fundamental matrix factorization in scientific computing and data analysis, but computing it efficiently on modern GPUs remains challenging. Full SVD provides strong numerical robustness but is often expensive for large matrices, whereas randomized SVD (RSVD) improves performance but may exhibit accuracy variability, especially when the target rank is unknown or the singular spectrum decays slowly. To address this challenge, we propose UnifaSVD, a unified and adaptive framework for high-performance and numerically reliable SVD on GPUs. UnifaSVD combines a numerically stable Householder QB (HQB) factorization for numerical rank estimation with a unified EVD-based SVD backend for efficient computation of the required singular values and vectors. Its adaptive architecture supports full-rank, low-rank, and unknown-rank matrices by dynamically selecting an appropriate computational path according to matrix characteristics and user-specified numerical requirements. Rather than relying on a fixed decomposition strategy, UnifaSVD integrates efficient factorization, adaptive rank handling, and lightweight refinement within a single framework. Experimental results show that UnifaSVD achieves numerical accuracy close to full SVD while delivering substantially higher performance across a wide range of tested cases. By automating algorithm selection based on matrix properties and numerical requirements, UnifaSVD provides a robust and efficient solution for SVD on modern GPU architectures.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: TCL: Enabling Fast and Efficient Cross-Hardware Tensor Program Optimization via Continual Learning
records.summary: Deep learning (DL) compilers rely on cost models and auto-tuning to optimize tensor programs for target hardware. However, existing approaches depend on large offline datasets, incurring high collection costs and offering suboptimal transferability across platforms. In this paper, we introduce TCL , a novel efficient and transferable compiler framework for fast tensor program optimization across diverse hardware platforms to address these challenges. Specifically, TCL is built on three core enablers: (1) the RDU Sampler , a data-efficient active learning strategy that selects only 10% of tensor programs by jointly optimizing R epresentativeness, D iversity, and U ncertainty, substantially reducing data collection costs while maintaining near-original model accuracy; (2) a new Mamba-based cost model that efficiently captures long-range schedule dependencies while achieving a favorable trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational cost through reduced parameterization and lightweight sequence modeling; and (3) a continuous knowledge distillation framework that effectively and progressively transfers knowledge across multiple hardware platforms while avoiding the parameter explosion and data dependency issues typically caused by traditional multi-task learning. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of each individual enabler and the holistic TCL framework. When optimizing a range of mainstream DL models on both CPU and GPU platforms, TCL achieves, on average, 16.8 × and 12.48 × faster tuning time, and 1.20 × and 1.13 × lower inference latency, respectively, compared to Tenset-MLP.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: MARS: Enabling Efficient DNN Mapping for Spatial Accelerators in Ruby Space
records.summary: Spatial accelerators can significantly enhance the computational performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) by mapping each layer across spatial and temporal dimensions. However, state-of-the-art mapping tools predominantly rely on perfect factorization mapping (PFM), which restricts tile sizes to exact divisors of tensor dimensions and may overlook high-quality mappings in the broader design space. To address this limitation, we propose MARS, the first efficient exploration framework designed for Ruby space. Ruby space is defined as a generalized mapping space that relaxes the factor-only constraint by allowing any integer tile size within the valid range of a dimension. MARS first models the coupling of partitioning, scheduling, and hardware resource constraints in Ruby space as a constrained optimization problem. It then relaxes the discrete mapping space into a continuous domain and employs a combination of linear programming and a genetic algorithm to rapidly obtain high-quality candidate mappings. Experimental results on representative DNN models show that MARS achieves a reduction of \(15\% \) to \(65\% \) in energy-delay product compared to state-of-the-art methods on average. Furthermore, MARS demonstrates superior exploration efficiency and consistently better mapping quality.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: JumpStart: Alleviating the Front-End Bottleneck in Modern x86 Processors
records.summary: With the stagnation of single-threaded performance, the need for optimizations targeting sequential code performance is greater than ever before. Modern workloads have also been growing in code footprint, exposing a bottleneck in the processor front-end, specifically its inability to maintain a sufficiently high fetch throughput to saturate available execution units. To address them, two optimizations exist in modern processors: (1) Fetch-Directed Instruction Prefetching (FDIP) and (2) the micro-op cache ( μ op cache), both of which improve fetch throughput leading to improved overall performance. However, since they target the same code regions, in the presence of FDIP, the μ op cache becomes mostly redundant as a performance optimization. This work proposes JumpStart : a novel and lightweight mechanism that synergistically exploits hints from FDIP to early-detect a μ op cache miss and wake up the decode pipeline ahead of time, alleviating a key front-end bottleneck.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: DMMU: SmartNIC-Based On-Device MMU for Scalable Virtualized I/O and Memory Overcommitment
records.summary: Cloud data centers increasingly rely on device virtualization to share high-bandwidth network adapters and accelerators among virtual machines (VMs). Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) exposes Virtual Functions (VFs) directly to guest VMs, but the Input/Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) on the host processor becomes a bottleneck as the number of VFs grows: its small translation lookaside buffer (TLB) causes severe throughput degradation. Meanwhile, because the hypervisor cannot determine which guest memory regions are used for Direct Memory Access (DMA), it must pin the entire VM memory, preventing memory overcommitment and wasting physical resources. Existing solutions, including Address Translation Services (ATS), the Page Request Interface (PRI), and software-emulated virtual IOMMUs, suffer from compatibility, deployment, or CPU overhead limitations. We propose DMMU, a Device MMU system implemented on programmable SmartNICs that addresses both the IOMMU translation bottleneck and the memory-pinning barrier to overcommitment, with minimal host software modification and zero guest awareness. DMMU introduces two techniques: combo-DMA , which dynamically routes address translations between the IOMMU and an on-device translation engine depending on IOMMU load, and direct-PRI , which enables the SmartNIC to issue page fault requests directly to a host-side driver, bypassing the multi-layer emulation path of conventional PRI in virtualized environments. We implement DMMU through a microcode update to a commodity dual-port 100G NIC and evaluate it on Intel Skylake and Ice Lake servers. With a representative 120-VF configuration, DMMU improves NIC throughput by 65% and reduces IOTLB misses by 38 × compared to the baseline IOMMU. DMMU also enables reliable memory overcommitment with device passthrough, achieving near-baseline Redis performance at a 1.35 × overcommitment ratio.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: AdaFuse: Adaptive Function Fusion for Dynamic Serverless Workflows
records.summary: Serverless workflows are commonly modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) composed of fine-grained functions. While this design promotes modularity and programming flexibility, it also incurs frequent inter-function communication. To alleviate this performance overhead, function fusion has been explored to co-locate and execute communicating functions within a shared container instance. However, existing approaches fail to account for the time-varying trade-off between communication latency reduction and resource overprovisioning arising from path uncertainty in dynamic serverless workflows, making it difficult to sustain high resource efficiency over time. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive function fusion strategy that dynamically reconstructs serverless workflows by adjusting communication schemes between functions in response to changing workflow invocations. Realizing this strategy, however, requires jointly optimizing function fusion and per-instance configuration, a problem with a combinatorial search space, while managing the substantial overhead of switching fusion schemes at runtime. To address these challenges, we design AdaFuse, a novel system for dynamic serverless workflows. AdaFuse jointly optimizes function fusion and instance reconfiguration through an efficient beam-search–based algorithm to optimize the end-to-end resource allocation. With the optimized fusion scheme, AdaFuse employs a fluid migration mechanism that incrementally transitions the workflow deployment while seamlessly redirecting incoming workloads. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show that AdaFuse reduces resource allocation by up to 49.4% compared to baselines, without compromising SLO attainment.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: LOAD: Enabling Low-Bit Group Quantization for Vision Transformers via Adaptive Data Formats
records.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve state-of-the-art performance across various vision tasks but pose significant deployment challenges due to their high computational complexity and memory footprint. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers an efficient, retraining-free compression strategy; however, existing solutions typically enforce a uniform quantization scheme (fixed bit-width and data format) across all layers, constraining the potential accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We propose LOAD-ViT , a novel PTQ framework that leverages both mixed-precision and mixed-data-format quantization to allocate resources at a fine granularity based on layer sensitivity. LOAD-ViT optimizes per-layer configurations via a calibration-based sensitivity metric and a constrained search algorithm, minimizing accuracy loss under strict hardware budgets. To support this scheme, we design a dedicated hardware accelerator featuring heterogeneous compute engines and lightweight format-conversion units, facilitating the efficient execution of mixed formats. Extensive evaluations on various ViT models and benchmarks demonstrate that LOAD-ViT achieves up to 5.3 × speedup and 4.2 × energy savings compared to state-of-the-art quantization accelerators, with negligible accuracy degradation.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
records.summary: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94GB s − 1 on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node.js 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6 × compared with Node.js 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: StrataJ: Enhancing File System Journaling Scalability via Adaptive Concurrency Control and Full-Stack Optimizations
records.summary: The scalability of file system journaling faces significant challenges due to the increasing concurrency demands of modern multi-core CPUs and high throughput NVMe SSDs. However, our study reveals that the concurrency of journaling should be carefully adjusted to the workload, and the underlying I/O stack must be customized to better support concurrent journaling. To address these challenges, we propose StrataJ , a full-stack journaling system designed to enhance scalability through cross-layered optimizations spanning the journaling, block I/O, and driver layers. First, we design an adaptive journaling layer that dynamically adjusts the number of journaling streams based on the real-time analysis of workloads. Second, we propose a scalable I/O control mechanism in the block layer, which eliminates contention by parallelizing writeback throttling and physical region page (PRP) management. Third, we develop a decentralized I/O virtual address (IOVA) management scheme in the driver layer, which enables different regions of the address space to flush cache independently, thus in parallel. Our evaluations show that StrataJ significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems across varied workloads, achieving up to 3.12 ×, 1.59 × and 2.30 × speedups on FxMark, Filebench, and RocksDB, respectively.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: ReHGNN: A Digital-Analog Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Sparse-Dense Matrix Multiplication in Hypergraph Neural Networks
records.summary: Resistive random access memory (ReRAM) based analog processing-in-memory (APIM) architectures have been extensively explored for accelerating matrix multiplication in various artificial neural networks (ANNs). However, since the emerging hypergraph neural network (HGNN) generally encompasses large and highly-sparse weight matrices, they usually results in a significant waste of ReRAM resource for zero values when HGNNs are processed with APIM. This paper presents ReHGNN, the first hybrid digital/analog PIM architecture for HGNN inference. We abstract most operations in the aggregation phase of HGNN as sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM), and explore a digital PIM (DPIM) to accelerate these SpMMs. First, we map only non-zero values of sparse matrices to DPIM arrays compactly to minimize the ReRAM resource consumption while improving computational parallelism. Second, we exploit heterogeneous crossbar arrays to accommodate the irregular distribution of sparse matrices. Third, we propose a greedy heuristic algorithm to further improve the utilization of ReRAM resource. Experimental results show that ReHGNN can improve the performance of HGNN inference by a factor of 3.4, 9.2, 15.3, 31.4, 41.3, and improve energy efficiency by a factor of 4.6, 14.1, 17.2, 363.8, and 473.4, compared with ReGNN, ReGraphX, FloatPIM, Hypergef, and GPUs, respectively.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Q-GMRES: Quantized Data Transmission Optimization for Distributed GMRES Algorithm
records.summary: The generalized minimal residual (GMRES) algorithm is one of the key iterative algorithms for solving large-scale sparse linear systems, which finds extensive application in scientific and engineering computations. Although distributed GMRES can handle large-scale problems, data transmission between multiple nodes emerges as a primary bottleneck. Given the inefficient utilization of finite bits in the IEEE 754 format and the potential impact of low-precision floating-point representations on the convergence of iterative algorithms, this paper proposes a quantization-based method (Q-GMRES) to compress the data transmitted between nodes. Our approach not only reduces the amount of data transmission, but also uses the limited bit-width representation to achieve high accuracy. In this paper, we explore uniform and non-uniform quantization techniques and propose inner-outer mixed-precision and vector segmentation methods to improve residual accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed communication compression method, which combines INT16 quantization with vector segmentation, achieves speedups of up to 2.19x and 2.49x on four and eight processes, respectively, while maintaining convergence accuracy comparable to GMRES-FP64.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: LSR: Eliminating Loop Control Overhead for Energy-Efficient Processors
records.summary: Loops constitute a small fraction of static code but dominate dynamic execution time and control overhead, posing significant challenges for energy-efficient mobile and embedded processors. This paper introduces Loop Semantic Recognition (LSR) , a microarchitectural technique that dynamically infers loop semantics to eliminate loop control overhead without requiring compiler support or ISA extensions. We further propose three complementary optimizations: Branch Strength Reduction (BSR), Hardware Loop Unrolling (HLU), and Stride Value Prediction (SVP), which progressively remove redundant control instructions, reduce pipeline pressure, and optimize loop execution. Evaluation on TSVC, PolyBench, NPB, and Swan benchmarks demonstrates that LSR and its extensions deliver substantial efficiency and energy benefits. HLU reduces committed instructions by up to 33.23% , while SVP lowers executed instructions by as much as 46.59% . LSR also reduces loop branch mispredictions and consistently decreases dynamic energy consumption, achieving an average processor-wide Energy-Delay Product (EDP) improvement of 8.36% across these four benchmark suites on a 2-wide baseline core. Scaling to a 4-wide core further raises the average EDP reduction to 15.39% . Additionally, LSR maintains consistent effectiveness across compiler optimization levels from -O1 to -O3 , confirming its robustness to code generation strategies. A complementary evaluation of SPEC CPU2017 shows an average EDP reduction of 2.93% , indicating that LSR optimization opportunities also exist in general-purpose workloads. These results are achieved with only 0.45 KB of total storage overhead, confirming LSR as a lightweight and practical solution for improving energy efficiency across mobile and embedded processor designs.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: LightZK: An Efficient GPU Acceleration Framework for Large-Scale Zero-Knowledge Proofs
records.summary: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs), particularly zk-SNARKs, have become a cornerstone for privacy-preserving protocols and blockchain scalability. However, the generation of proofs remains computationally prohibitive due to the immense overhead of underlying cryptographic primitives, namely Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) and Fast Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). As applications scale up to billion-scale constraints, conventional GPU-accelerated frameworks tailored for smaller instances suffer from overwhelming memory usage, invalid architectural assumptions, and suboptimal end-to-end orchestration. Driven by the motivation to complete massive proof generation on a single memory-constrained node, this paper presents LightZK, an efficient GPU acceleration framework for large-scale zero-knowledge proofs based on a tile-based execution model. LightZK not only aims to support ultra-large-scale ZKP generation, but also strives to improve the practical performance of proof generation. LightZK contributes a micro-architectural diagnosis of MSM on GPUs: hardware performance counters expose the register-pressure and low instruction-level-parallelism mismatches that under-utilize the GPU during bucket-merge computation, and targeted kernel optimizations derived from this diagnosis yield a 1.5 × –2.5 × MSM speedup over the SOTA baseline. LightZK further makes large-scale NTT executable where the SOTA GPU baseline fails, via storage and structural optimizations that deliver nontrivial acceleration (2.2 × –2.5 × over a functional baseline). At the systemic level, LightZK builds on a data-dependency graph (DDG) analysis of the Groth16 proving flow to drive a three-tier pipeline orchestration: a hand-crafted DRAM-VRAM pipeline for Poly-phase that overlaps sparse matrix operations with data transfer, and a producer-consumer disk-DRAM-VRAM pipeline for Group-phase that treats each MSM tile as an independently schedulable unit. Experimental results demonstrate that LightZK achieves a 2.8 × end-to-end performance improvement over the leading executable GPU baseline at standard scales. Crucially, while existing GPU frameworks exceed available memory at billion-scale, LightZK successfully sustains 2 30 -scale proof generation with near-linear scalability on a single node.
records.journalName: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

records.title: Adaptive Thread Scheduling and Optimization Framework for the Multi-Core CPU with Large-Capacity Cache
records.summary: The continuous growth in processor speed and the persistent memory latency bottleneck make large-capacity cache critical for mitigating the “memory wall”. However, topology-oblivious OS scheduling frequently induces severe cache contention and cross-die migrations, diminishing these hardware benefits. To address this, we propose a thread scheduling framework driven by runtime microarchitectural feedback. Instead of treating performance profiling and thread placement as isolated steps, our approach directly uses hardware performance counters to guide thread configurations to maximize cache utilization. First, the Thread and CPU Monitoring (TCM) framework tracks CPU and cache contention across both Simultaneous Multi-Threading (SMT) and non-SMT modes. Based on this feedback, the Thread Extension and Placement (TEP) algorithm dynamically adapts thread concurrency. To balance computational efficiency and runtime overhead, TEP determines the optimal thread count using cubic spline interpolation combined with a golden ratio search. Concurrently, a topology-aware affinity strategy binds threads to specific cores to maintain cache locality. Evaluations on AMD EPYC processors show that this approach improves overall execution efficiency. On average, the framework reduces the L3 miss rate from 62.71% to 51.89%, lowers CPI from 2.35 to 2.02, decreases cross-core thread migrations from 36902 to 33339, and reduces wall-clock time by 10.52%. The framework operates in user space without kernel modifications, ensuring ease of practical deployment for HPC and AI inference.

records.title: Rigorous Evaluation of Microarchitectural Side-Channels with Statistical Model Checking
records.summary: Rigorous quantitative evaluation of microarchitectural side channels is challenging for two reasons. First, the processors, attacks, and defenses often exhibit probabilistic behaviors. These probabilistic behaviors arise due to natural noise in systems (e.g., from co-running processes), probabilistic side channel attacks, and probabilistic obfuscation defenses. Second, microprocessors are extremely complex. Previous evaluation methods have relied on abstract or simplified models, which are necessarily less detailed than real systems or cycle-by-cycle simulators, and these models may miss important phenomena. Whereas a simple model may suffice for estimating performance, security issues frequently manifest in the details. We address this challenge by introducing Statistical Model Checking (SMC) to the quantitative evaluation of microarchitectural side channels. SMC is a rigorous statistical technique that can process the results of probabilistic experiments and provide statistical guarantees, and it has been used in computing applications that depend heavily on statistical guarantees (e.g., medical implants, vehicular computing). With SMC, we can treat processors as opaque boxes, and we do not have to abstract or simplify them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SMC through three case studies, in which we experimentally show that SMC can evaluate existing security vulnerabilities and defenses and provide qualitatively similar conclusions with greater statistical rigor, while making no simplifying assumptions or abstractions. We also show that SMC can enable a defender to quantify the amount of noise necessary to have a desired level of confidence that she has reduced an attacker’s probability of success to less than a desired threshold, thus providing the defender with an actionable plan for obfuscation via noise injection.

records.title: PCR: A Prefetch-Enhanced Cache Reuse System for Low-Latency RAG Serving
records.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly improves Large Language Models (LLMs) but introduces massive input sequences that severely bottleneck the prefill stage. While KV-cache reuse reduces redundant computation for shared document prefixes, the reusable KV working set in RAG serving can exceed GPU memory capacity, requiring KV chunks to be retained across host DRAM and SSDs. However, naive multi-tier storage extensions suffer from severe I/O bottlenecks, suboptimal eviction, and high CPU-GPU data transfer overheads, which often negate the latency benefits of cache reuse. In this paper, we propose PCR, a P refetch-enhanced C ache R euse system for low-latency RAG serving. PCR transforms passive SSD-backed storage into an active, latency-hiding memory hierarchy through three core modules: (1) a Multi-Tier Prefix-Tree Cache Manager that unifies the organization and tracking of reusable KV chunks across the entire memory hierarchy of GPU, host DRAM, and SSD; (2) a Queue-Guided Runtime Scheduler that leverages the post-retrieval waiting queue as a look-ahead signal to proactively protect hot chunks and prefetch SSD-resident data into host DRAM before execution; and (3) a Latency-Hiding KV Transfer Pipeline that overlaps fine-grained PCIe data movement and asynchronous SSD operations with model computation. Extensive evaluations across diverse models and RAG workloads show that PCR reduces TTFT over the evaluated KV-cache reuse systems in most settings, with a 2.45 × speedup over vLLM for Llama3.1-8B on A6000 under Workload 1 at 1.0 request/s, while maintaining lower tail latency under high load.

records.title: DPSM: Fine-Grained GPU Resource Management via Kernel Interception and TPC Control
records.summary: Modern deep learning workloads are increasingly co-located on a single GPU to improve hardware utilization, yet existing MPS-based sharing mechanisms expose concurrency without providing QoS-aware control. Deadline-constrained training jobs can suffer severe slowdown when co-executed with best-effort workloads, because MPS does not reason about job urgency or deadline slack. This paper presents DPSM, a transparent runtime system for QoS-first, throughput-aware co-scheduling of concurrent deep learning jobs on a single NVIDIA GPU. DPSM does not replace the native GPU scheduler, generate deadlines, or assign deadlines to individual kernels. Instead, it intercepts CUDA kernel launches, tracks job-level progress and slowdown online, and identifies the most urgent job using a slack-based scoring model. DPSM then enforces the scheduling decision through two complementary mechanisms: launch-timing control for large-grid best-effort kernels, and TPC-mask control that limits the TPC budget of selected small-grid best-effort kernels. Under MPS, DPSM treats TPC masks as budget controls that limit the number of available TPCs. This design preserves the MPS execution model while mitigating temporal and resource-budget interference among co-running jobs. We evaluate DPSM on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs using representative two-job and three-job deep learning co-location workloads. Across 1260 job-deadline instances, DPSM achieves the highest all-job deadline completion rate (DCR) of 39.2%, compared with 37.6% for TGS, 28.7% for MPS, and 18.6% for Orion. DPSM also maintains competitive normalized iteration throughput of 0.471, close to the highest-throughput baseline Orion at 0.499, while providing substantially better deadline satisfaction. We envision DPSM as a valuable tool for the community and have open-sourced it to facilitate future research at https://github.com/HIT-CeeCG/DPSM.

records.title: Nephele: Bridging DDR–CXL Latency Gaps with Benefit-Aware Caching for In-Memory Databases on Hybrid Memory
records.summary: In-memory databases rely on DDR memory for performance, yet capacity scaling is impeded by physical constraints and the high cost of high-density DIMMs. Compute Express Link (CXL) provides a practical path for memory expansion through a DDR-compatible interface. However, CXL memory exhibits inferior latency and bandwidth, thus naïve expansion with CXL can lead to significant performance degradation. In hybrid DDR–CXL systems, traditional caching policies (e.g., LRU, S3-FIFO) yield limited reductions in execution latency while incurring substantial metadata management and tuple migration overheads. Our analysis reveals a fundamental misalignment between traditional design assumptions and heterogeneous memory characteristics. To address this, we propose Nephele, a lightweight, benefit-aware caching policy for hybrid DDR–CXL databases. Nephele shifts the focus from eviction selection to effective admission, prioritizing data that are truly worth caching. It also features a low-overhead architecture that supports randomized eviction without relying on global metadata. By integrating epoch-based hotness estimation, Nephele enables probabilistic, benefit-aware admission, reducing cross-tier data movement and mitigating cache pollution. Evaluated on a hybrid DDR–CXL database prototype using YCSB and TPC-C, Nephele achieves up to 1.58× higher throughput than CXL-Expansion and up to 3.2× over existing caching policies, while retaining up to 97% of DDR-only performance. Additional integration with RocksDB further confirms its practical feasibility in a production system. These results demonstrate that lightweight, benefit-aware caching is critical for fully exploiting CXL-enabled memory expansion.

records.title: A Bandwidth-Balanced Adaptive Technique for Mesh-Based I/O Chiplets
records.summary: As the semiconductor industry rapidly embraces chiplet-based architectures to satisfy AI-driven high-performance computing demands, the flexible, scalable I/O‑Die (IOD) chiplet offers a promising path toward solving the AI memory wall. However, the design of these IOD chiplets for flexibility and reuse across products dictates a fixed peripheral placement for all memory controllers and die-to-die interfaces, creating unique and largely unexplored challenges. This rigid layout causes severe, non-uniform congestion in the mesh-based Network-on-Chip (NoC), underutilizing its full cross-sectional bandwidth and forming a critical system-level performance bottleneck. To address this, we propose the Bandwidth Balanced Adaptive Technique (BBAT) that diversifies traffic across the mesh paths using a probabilistic routing hint updated online from measured congestion. Unlike prior adaptive techniques, BBAT’s core innovation is a feedback mechanism that leverages the existing high-performance cache-coherent transaction protocol, eliminating the need for custom signaling. To dynamically adapt to shifting traffic patterns, our technique employs simple, low-overhead hardware logic that processes both traditional and novel congestion metrics gathered from across the chiplet—a design optimized for high performance while maintaining power efficiency. We conduct an extensive evaluation using a cycle-accurate simulator across two distinct chiplet topologies—one modeled after a commercial, asymmetric IOD and another with a uniform interface layout. The results demonstrate that our technique achieves a peak performance improvement of 2.6 × over the Dimension-Ordered Routing (DOR) baseline in synthetic traffic and outperforms prior congestion-aware adaptive approaches by up to 14% under heavily congested synthetic patterns. Across a practical mix of synthetic traffic patterns evaluated on both topologies, BBAT consistently delivers a 1.1 × –1.8 × speedup relative to the deterministic DOR baseline. Critically, on memory-bound SPEC CPU2017 workloads, it achieves a 1.2 × –1.7 × speedup over DOR and 7–10% higher throughput than existing adaptive techniques, demonstrating effective load balancing and strong congestion responsiveness in high-performance chiplet architectures, while adding only 5.4% to total NoC area.
